questions.rationale: BP 344 and PD 1096 are the local source-supported design references for accessible facility dimensions.

questions.text: What minimum clear width does the 2024 BP 344 IRR give for accessible ramps?
questions.rationale: The 2024 BP 344 IRR states a 1200 mm minimum clear width for accessible ramps.
questions.explanation: This question tests the 25% additional wage deduction for PWD employees — frequently confused with the 50% accessibility improvement deduction, which is a different incentive.

questions.text: Which law explicitly criminalizes the public ridicule and vilification of PWDs, and what type of provision does it insert into RA 7277?

options.text: RA 10754 — it inserts a tax penalty clause for businesses that ridicule PWD customers
RA 9442 — it inserts specific penal provisions on public ridicule and vilification into RA 7277
BP 344 — it adds anti-ridicule provisions as part of the 2024 IRR update to the Accessibility Law
RA 7277 itself — the original Magna Carta already contained anti-ridicule criminal penalties at enactment

questions.rationale: RA 9442 (2007) inserts specific penal provisions on public ridicule and vilification into RA 7277. RA 9442, enacted in 2007 as an amendment to RA 7277, adds explicit penal provisions criminalizing public ridicule and vilification of PWDs. These provisions recognize that discrimination against PWDs extends beyond physical access barriers to include social humiliation and degrading treatment. RA 10754 (2016) focuses on financial benefits (VAT exemption, expanded discounts) and does not add anti-ridicule provisions.
questions.explanation: This question tests which law added the anti-ridicule criminal provisions — a distinction between RA 9442 (anti-discrimination, anti-ridicule) and RA 10754 (financial benefits).

questions.text: What is the source-safe interpretation of a 1500 mm sidewalk or walkway requirement?

options.text: It is a PWD VAT exemption rule
It is an accessibility-route dimension supported by BP 344
It is a business permit penalty
It is a tax deduction limit

questions.rationale: BP 344 supports sidewalk and walkway widths as accessibility-route dimensions, not benefit-law provisions.
questions.explanation: This question enforces the law-dimension separation principle — RA 10754 = benefits and penalties; BP 344 = physical specifications. A critical distinction for the LEA.

questions.text: When two wheelchair users need to pass on a sidewalk or walkway, what width does the 2024 BP 344 IRR identify?
questions.rationale: The 2024 BP 344 IRR gives 1800 mm where space is required for two wheelchairs to pass.
questions.explanation: This question tests the 1% government employment quota under RA 10524 — a specific figure tested as a straightforward recall item on the LEA.

questions.text: What should an architect do with PWD discount, VAT, employment quota, tax incentive, or penalty claims when the local RA/BIR source packet is unavailable?

options.text: Use BP 344 dimensions as proof of those benefits
Defer or narrow the item until the local law packet is acquired

questions.rationale: Privilege-law claims require their own verified local source packet; the safe batch action is to defer those claims or narrow to locally supported accessibility design.
questions.explanation: This question tests the 50% additional deduction for above-minimum accessibility improvements — and the critical condition that it applies only to expenditures beyond what BP 344 already mandates.

questions.text: What handrail heights are supported in the local accessibility source family?
questions.rationale: PD 1096 Appendix A and the BP 344 source family support handrails at 0.70 m and 0.90 m above ramps or steps.
questions.explanation: This law-separation question tests whether candidates correctly route physical specifications to BP 344 IRR — not to RA 7277/9442/10754, which govern rights and benefits.

questions.text: What minimum clear width does the 2024 BP 344 IRR give for accessible ramps?

questions.explanation: This foundational recall question tests the correct law name and year for the Magna Carta — commonly confused with its amendments RA 9442 and RA 10754.

questions.text: Tracing the penalty evolution across the PWD law amendments, what is the current maximum criminal fine under the most recent law (RA 10754) for violations of PWD privileges and accessibility provisions?

options.text: ₱50,000 — the original BP 344 penalty, still in effect as the primary accessibility enforcement fine, despite subsequent amendments
₱100,000 — the RA 7277 Sec. 46 penalty, which superseded the original BP 344 fine, reflecting an increase in enforcement measures
₱200,000 — the RA 9442 amendment penalty, updated in 2007 to address inflation and increased enforcement needs
₱300,000 — the RA 10754 maximum, the current controlling standard with up to 6 years imprisonment

questions.rationale: The current maximum criminal fine is ₱300,000 under RA 10754, combined with up to 6 years imprisonment — the most recent amendment controls. The penalty evolution: BP 344 original = ₱50,000 (no jail term); RA 7277 Sec. 46 = ₱100,000 + 6 months to 2 years; RA 9442 amendment = ₱200,000 + 6 months to 6 years; RA 10754 amendment = ₱300,000 + up to 6 years. The most recent law (RA 10754, 2016) controls. The ₱50,000 original BP 344 penalty is the most common distractor — it is frequently offered as an answer because candidates remember seeing it in BP 344, not realizing it has been superseded.
questions.explanation: This question tests the penalty progression across all four laws and requires candidates to select the highest (RA 10754) as the current controlling standard.
